Headless only: the --test suite.. Judge: One side won all four pairs clearly, and none was indistinguishable. Each winning frame (pair 1 B; pair 2, 3 and 4 A) has three things the other lacks: dense, lived-in set dressing; hard, directional light that grounds people and props with crisp shadows; and staging, meaning a hero car or a story beat that frames the walking figure. Pair 2 A and pair 4 A genuinely wowed me. The losing frames, all from the same Singapore-set game, have good bones: believable skies and sun direction, a landmark skyline, rain trees, convincing shophouse and apartment-block facades, Peranakan tiles. They keep failing in the same ways. The plaza foregrounds are bare, with soft, blotchy tile textures. The main character is a stylized, low-detail avatar whose mid-stride poses look awkward when frozen in a still (a lunge, crossed legs on tiptoe). The background people are copies of the hero's model. Several surfaces are untextured blockout: the awning plane, the utility cabinets, and slabs that seem to float. Lighting on the characters is flat, with weak contact shadows. A small world-space bug: a street-name label runs past its sign plate. The fixes that would gain most, in order: dress and add detail to the ground plane, finish or replace the blockout geometry, add character variety and fidelity, and stage shots around a hero prop. Protocol note: 2 of the 8 images (pair-1 B and pair-3 A) carry a game-title logo in the corner, which reveals their source and breaks the blinding. All the winning frames also look like posed press stills, while the others look like raw gameplay captures. I judged only the rendered content, but the logos should be cropped or masked in future rounds. Composition comparisons are also tilted toward posed stills, though the gaps I listed above are real either way.
